title: One Canadian Economy, Thirteen Rulebooks: What Interprovincial Trucking Harmonization Actually Changed
summary: Canada's 2026 trucking MOU aligned steer axles, permit standards and oversize rules. What still differs by province, and how carriers and brokers encode it.
body_markdown:
A Winnipeg-based fleet quotes a customer a dedicated lane into Saskatchewan and Alberta for next spring. The rate assumes full legal weights, because the planner read the headlines: Canada passed an internal trade law, the provinces signed a trucking agreement, the rules are being aligned. In late March the first loads hit secondary highways under spring weight restrictions, the trucks run light or detour, and the margin on the contract disappears in six weeks. Nothing in the planner's reading was wrong. It was just about a different layer of the rulebook.


That is the operating problem with harmonization in 2026. A lot really did change. Much more did not, and the parts that did not are exactly the ones that hit a load plan, a permit request or a quote. The decision for carriers and brokers is not whether to believe the harmonization story. It is which rules to retire from your workflow and which ones to keep enforcing, province by province.


## What the federal law did, and what it could not do


The headline law is real. Bill C-5, the One Canadian Economy Act, received Royal Assent on June 26, 2025. Its Free Trade and Labour Mobility in Canada Act came into force on January 1, 2026, under an order published in the Canada Gazette in November 2025. The Act's approach is mutual recognition: Ottawa accepts comparable provincial or territorial requirements as meeting federal ones for goods, services and labour moving within Canada. On June 30, 2025, the federal government also announced it was removing all of its remaining exceptions to the Canadian Free Trade Agreement, eliminating all 53 since the agreement took effect in 2017. Intergovernmental Affairs reported that between January 1, 2025 and the November 19, 2025 Committee on Internal Trade meeting, governments together removed 94 of 296 exceptions, about 30%.


For trucking, the limit is jurisdiction. The rules that shape a load plan day to day, such as axle weights on provincial highways, oversize permits, seasonal restrictions and carrier safety ratings, are mostly provincial and territorial. The federal Act removes federal barriers. It does not rewrite a province's highway traffic regulations.


The trucking-specific work runs through a separate track: the transportation ministers and the national safety code body.


## The 14-measure trucking MOU, measured in operating terms


On June 12, 2026, the Council of Ministers Responsible for Transportation and Highway Safety announced the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding on Interprovincial Trucking covering 14 measures. Signatures run from November 2025 into early 2026, and every province and territory plus Ottawa is a party. The MOU itself states it is not legally binding and does not affect any party's jurisdiction. Any party can suspend a commitment for reasons including extreme weather and infrastructure damage.


### Changes that are mostly done


**Steering axle weight.** The MOU commits all provinces and territories to amend the national weights and dimensions agreement to raise the steering axle limit from 5,500 kg to 6,000 kg. Its implementation table lists British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador and Yukon as completed. New Brunswick's regulatory amendment was scheduled for late fall or winter 2026, and Prince Edward Island listed 2026 as an estimate. If you spec heavier front ends for Atlantic work, the last two provinces are still the binding constraint.


**Oversize and overweight minimum standards.** A March 2026 annex of minimum national standards covers signage, lighting and flags for oversized vehicles, escort vehicle equipment and driver qualifications, construction zone lane clearance of 3.5 m on freeways or routes with regular truck traffic, and a common day and night definition for time-of-day restrictions on oversize moves: daylight begins 30 minutes before sunrise, and nighttime begins 30 minutes after sunset, using National Research Council sunrise and sunset times for the vehicle's location. Before this, the MOU notes, Alberta defined daytime as starting one hour before sunrise, while Ontario used 30 minutes.


**Permit service standards.** Each province and territory committed to publish oversize and overweight permit service standards by March 31, 2026, and the national task force committed to a common set of application data elements. Manitoba, for example, now publishes targets of one business day for annual blanket permits and for permit office review of one-move permits, two business days for internal approval up to 100,000 kg gross, and ten business days above that, with a goal of meeting the standard on at least 70% of applications.


**A single reference point.** The Canadian Trucking Regulations Hub, led by Alberta with all jurisdictions contributing data, went live on April 22, 2026, with jurisdiction comparisons, route planning, a weight calculator and permit office information. Each jurisdiction maintains its own data, and the hub labels itself for information purposes only. Alberta said long-term management was expected to move to the Canadian Council of Motor Transport Administrators (CCMTA) in fall 2026.


### Changes still in progress


**Safety standards.** The MOU's National Safety Code annex committed CCMTA to revise NSC 7 (carrier and driver profiles), NSC 14 (safety rating) and NSC 15 (facility audits), with provinces aiming to implement within two years of ministerial approval. In a July 23, 2026 update, CCMTA said it would present the revisions to deputy ministers in fall 2026 and to ministers after that. The work includes tighter carrier number applications, better detection of carriers that change names or jurisdictions, and a rebuilt interprovincial carrier data exchange. A separate review of safety rating processes under NSC 14 is expected by the end of 2026. Quebec's entry says it will contribute "without any possible commitment on a possible schedule."


**Entry-level training.** Provinces and territories without entry-level training consistent with NSC 16 committed to implement it by December 31, 2027.


**Long combination vehicles.** LCV rules remain regional by design. The MOU says eastern provinces (Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia) and western jurisdictions harmonize separately because LCVs cannot cross northern Ontario. On dangerous goods that do not require an emergency response assistance plan, Ontario allows them in LCVs while Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick did not, and Quebec's timeline is listed as "to be determined."


### Things the MOU explicitly leaves alone


The infrastructure annex says that under the existing weights and dimensions agreement, a truck "can be configured to move across Canada without barriers," and treats that harmonization as achieved. The 60 ft 6 in trailer annex sets a national guideline only for jurisdictions that choose to allow those trailers. Seasonal weight restrictions are not in scope at all.


## What still differs, province to province


**Seasonal restrictions.** Saskatchewan started 2026 spring weight restrictions on southern secondary highways on March 20, cutting allowable weights on those highways and rural municipal roads by 10% to 15% for up to six weeks. Rural municipalities set their own limits. Manitoba's 2026 order ran restrictions in five climate zones, starting March 20 in Zone 1 and ending between May 19 and May 31 depending on zone. Ontario's reduced load periods ran March 1 to April 30 on Schedule 1 highways, to May 31 on Schedule 2, and to June 30 on listed local roads. Ontario also made annual and project overload permits invalid in March and April in the south and through May in the north. Three neighbouring provinces, three calendars.


**Permits.** Service standards are now published, but they are targets. Each jurisdiction keeps full discretion over approval, required information and conditions. The MOU says so directly. Escort requirements still vary in practice, including where police escorts are required.


**Electronic logging.** The federal ELD requirement covers drivers crossing provincial or territorial borders, with enforcement from January 1, 2023. Coverage for intra-provincial work is a provincial choice. Ontario, for example, has required certified ELDs for certain intra-provincial truck drivers since June 12, 2022, with fines of $250 to $20,000, and it applies those requirements to out-of-province plates operating in Ontario.


**Safety ratings.** Until revised NSC standards are approved and implemented, each jurisdiction runs its own audit and rating model and the profile follows the carrier's base jurisdiction. Harmonization here is at least two years from operating reality once ministers sign off.


## How asset, broker and hybrid operators should respond


**Asset carriers** gain the most from the parts that are finished. Spec equipment to the 6,000 kg steer axle limit where it is in force, and treat New Brunswick and PEI as exceptions until their amendments land. The bigger cost exposure is seasonal. Spring restriction calendars should be lane attributes, versioned by year and by zone, and quoting for March through June should check them before the rate goes out. A fleet in an NSC audit cycle should assume the current provincial model applies through at least 2027.


**Brokers** carry the risk differently. You do not choose the equipment, but you choose the carrier and the promise to the shipper. A shipper who reads "harmonized" may expect full weights in April on a Saskatchewan secondary highway. Your tender should say otherwise. For oversize freight, published permit service standards give you a defensible lead time to quote: use the posted standard plus a buffer, and record which jurisdiction's standard you relied on. Carrier vetting benefits from tracking base jurisdiction and safety rating separately, since the coming NSC revisions are aimed squarely at carriers that reappear under new names or new provinces.


**Hybrids** face the coordination problem. Brokered and asset loads on the same lane should not use different restriction calendars or permit assumptions. Keep one source of truth per jurisdiction, with a named owner and a fixed refresh calendar: spring orders in February and March, permit standards when they change, NSC status when ministers act.


## Encode the differences, do not memorize them


Harmonization moves at the speed of the slowest jurisdiction, and some differences are permanent by design. The practical response is to stop treating provincial rules as tribal knowledge and put them where decisions get made. Every operation's mix of lanes, equipment and customers is different, so the rules that matter will be different too.


In practice that means jurisdiction rules attached to lanes and orders, with seasonal date ranges that block or flag a load at entry. Status steps that will not let an oversize load move to dispatched until every permit on the route is recorded. Permissions over who can override a weight or restriction flag, and why. Billing rules that handle permit, escort and detour costs consistently with each contract. Visibility that shows the shipper why a March load is lighter than a January one. Capacity logic that knows which equipment is legal on which routes and when.


The 2026 agreements made the map simpler. They did not make it uniform. The operators who profit are the ones whose systems know the difference.


## FAQ


### Did the One Canadian Economy Act harmonize trucking rules across provinces?


No, it removed federal barriers to internal trade, not provincial trucking rules. The Free Trade and Labour Mobility in Canada Act took effect January 1, 2026 and recognizes comparable provincial requirements as meeting federal ones, but weights, permits, seasonal restrictions and safety ratings remain mostly provincial.


### What is the 2026 Memorandum of Understanding on Interprovincial Trucking?


It is a non-binding agreement among all federal, provincial and territorial transportation ministers covering 14 trucking measures, announced June 12, 2026. It includes a 6,000 kg steering axle limit, oversize and escort minimum standards, published permit service standards, LCV training alignment, an NSC review and a national trucking regulations hub.


### Is the 6,000 kg steering axle limit in force everywhere in Canada?


Not yet. The MOU's implementation table lists most provinces and Yukon as completed, but New Brunswick scheduled its amendment for late fall or winter 2026 and Prince Edward Island estimated 2026.


### Are spring weight restrictions harmonized between provinces?


No, spring and seasonal restrictions are outside the MOU and are still set by each province, and often by municipalities. In 2026, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario each used different start dates, end dates, zones and reductions.


### When will National Safety Code safety ratings be harmonized?


Not before 2027 at the earliest. CCMTA planned to bring revised NSC 7, 14 and 15 to deputy ministers in fall 2026, and provinces aim to implement within two years of ministerial approval, so the current provincial rating models still apply.
